item.title: Floodwaters Overwhelm Thailand
item.summary: Heavy rains since mid-September have caused widespread flooding that has affected millions of people across the country.
item.page_text:
Heavy rains since mid-September have caused widespread flooding that has affected millions of people across the country.
September falls in the heart of the monsoon season in Thailand, where cities and towns are accustomed to the afternoon rains and thunderstorms that frequently roll through. But throughout late September and early October 2026, persistent heavy rains punctuated by intense downpours left low-lying areas across the country in Southeast Asia under sustained flooding.
Prachin Buri province was among the areas where flooding was widespread. The right image above shows land along the Bang Pakong River and nearby agricultural areas and aquaculture facilities inundated on October 2, 2026. The left image shows the same area at the same time of year in 2025. Acquired with NASA-USGS Landsat satellites, the images are false-color to better distinguish water from vegetation, developed land, and other surfaces. The bright red shapes are floating solar arrays.
Some of the flooding likely stemmed from a low-pressure system that stalled over the area for several days in late September. Stoked by moisture and energy from the warm Gulf of Thailand nearby, the system delivered especially intense rains to the region. About 100 kilometers (60 miles) to the west, Bangkok received nearly 300 millimeters (11.8 inches) of rain over a 48-hour period, according to news reports, close to the average monthly rainfall total for September of 344 millimeters (13.5 inches).
Since mid-September, flooding has occurred in 50 provinces across the country, affecting over 4 million people and causing dozens of deaths, according to the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies . Government agencies estimate about 270,000 hectares (670,000 acres) of farmland, including rice fields and fruit orchards, have been damaged.

item.page_text:
The third satellite launched on the Copernicus Sentinel-3 mission delivers its captivating first images
The very first image stretches from southern Germany to North Africa, with Italy and the Mediterranean Sea at its centre under largely clear skies. Captured from 30 September, a little over two weeks after launch on 15 September , the first preliminary images also cover Arctic sea ice, turquoise seas around the Bahamas, North Atlantic sea levels and the Antarctic ice sheet. The satellite’s observations will support forecasts at sea, monitor health of aquatic ecosystems and carbon pools, enable rapid response to wildfires and harmful algal blooms, and track sea level rises and ice melt.
“These stunning first images show that Copernicus Sentinel-3C is performing superbly just a few weeks after launch,” said Milen Tahtadjiev, Copernicus Sentinel-3 Mission Manager at EUMETSAT. “In a year of record sea-surface temperatures, an exceptional El Niño and a summer of drought and wildfires across Europe, Sentinel-3C will extend the vital record needed to track such changes, helping to save lives, protect livelihoods and strengthen economies. After years of preparation, the whole EUMETSAT team is delighted to see the satellite delivering its first observations. Over the coming months, the satellite and its instruments will be carefully tested and calibrated, so that its data can begin flowing to users across Europe and the world.”
The first image, captured on 30 September 2026 at about 09:30 UTC, is one of three released from the Ocean and Land Colour Instrument (OLCI), which records sunlight reflected from Earth’s surface in 21 bands of colour, enabling experts to pick out features just a few hundred metres across. Its data are used to monitor water quality, estimate how much carbon the ocean takes up, enable a rapid response to harmful algal blooms and assess how crops are growing on land.
The image stretches from southern Germany to the northern tip of Tunisia and covers parts of the Mediterranean Sea, Central Europe and the Western Balkans, from Austria and Hungary to the Croatian coast. On 30 September, a large area of high pressure sat over Europe, trapping warm air beneath it and bringing clear skies and summer-like temperatures unusually late in the year. Most of Italy is under clear skies, with clouds moving in from the west, while snow is visible on the high Alps.
Along the Italian Adriatic coast, a thin band of green and turquoise marks water coloured by sediment and phytoplankton, the microscopic organisms that form the base of marine food webs but can also be harmful. Severe drought in 2026 impacted delicate marine environments and accelerated the growth of aggressive algae that suffocated local coastal ecosystems. To the east, Lake Balaton shows pale green in western Hungary: after a summer drought, the lake’s water level was close to its record low in late September.
Far to the north, another OLCI image looks across the Canadian Arctic, including the northern end of Baffin Island – the fifth largest island in the world – and Lancaster Sound, the eastern entrance to the Northwest Passage. Smooth white ice caps and snow-covered mountains stand out against the dark, open water of the channels between the islands. Across much of the top half of the image, the waters are strewn with fragmented sea ice.
The Bahamas, Cuba, Haiti and the Dominican Republic appear in a third OLCI image. The palest blues are the Bahama Banks, where sunlight reflects off white sand through water only a few metres deep. Long-term global sea-level rise slowly deepens the submerged flats and alters interior tidal marshes and mudflats across the islands. The dark blue channel beside Andros, the largest island in the Bahamas, is the Tongue of the Ocean, a trench up to 2,000 metres deep. Large clusters of cloud hang over the warm sea, in a hurricane season that had produced eight named storms but no full-blown hurricanes by the end of September – a lull meteorologists have linked to El Niño.
Where OLCI records colour, the satellite’s Synthetic Aperture Radar Altimeter (SRAL) measures height, timing radar pulses bounced off the surface to determine sea levels to within a few centimetres and track how they rise over time. Its observations are also used to derive wave height and wind speed, which support shipping and marine forecasts, and the thickness of sea ice, a key indicator of climate change. Over land, they give the height of rivers and lakes, helping authorities manage water supplies and monitor floods and droughts.
SRAL’s first measurements are shown as a track across the North Atlantic, covering the first five days after the activation of the instrument (30 September – 4 October 2026). Unlike a camera, the altimeter observes only the narrow strip of sea directly beneath it, taking a reading roughly every 300 metres to build up a line of precise measurements.
The sea is not level: warm water expands and currents pile water up, leaving some areas a few tens of centimetres higher or lower than usual and marking out currents such as the Gulf Stream, which helps to shape Europe’s weather and climate. The colours show how far the sea surface stood above or below its long-term average, which is calculated from a reference period of 20 years of measurements (1993-2012).
The track is laid over a map from the Copernicus Marine Service, implemented by Mercator Ocean International, that combines observations from several altimetry satellites in a single dataset. The colours match, showing that the new satellite’s first data are consistent with those from satellites already in orbit.
Other imagery from the first set of SRAL observations have been used to produce an animation of the ice sheet in Greenland. The Greenland ice sheet is the second-largest ice mass on Earth after Antarctica, and its losses are a growing contributor to global sea-level rise. item.title: Image of the week: Dust cloud moves over the Mediterranean
item.summary: Image of the week: Dust cloud moves over the Mediterranean Sarah Leach Fri, 09/10/2026 - 09:00 Image of the week: Dust cloud moves over the Mediterranean Watching our Earth from space This week’s image is of Saharan dust moving northeast across the Mediterranean Sea on 25 August 2026. The image was captured by the Meteosat-12 geostationary weather satellite 36,000km above the Earth. Last Updated Published on Saharan dust particles are lifted into the atmosphere by gusts of surface wind and can be transported and deposited thousands of kilometres away. When dust travels over populated areas, it can reduce air quality and impact health by causing respiratory problems and cause flight delays. Over the oceans, dust can act as a fertiliser, stimulating blooms of tiny marine plants (phytoplankton) that are the basis for the marine food chain. The latest imagery from Meteosat-12 can be accessed on EUMETView . Dust image This image was captured by the FCI instrument onboard Meteosat-12 on 25 August 2026. The Meteosat weather satellites provide imagery for the early detection of fast-developing severe weather, weather forecasting and climate monitoring. More info Access Meteosat-12 imagery

item.title: Unlocking Earth AI’s planetary geospatial foundation models for global public health
item.page_text:
Arbaaz Muslim, Software Engineer, Google Research, and Gautam Prasad, Software Engineer, Google Research
With Google Earth AI’s Population Dynamics Foundation Model (PDFM), we can address the data gaps and temporal reporting lags of existing epidemiological workflows. In our latest work, we present five partner-driven case studies demonstrating how this model exemplifies the planetary geospatial foundation model paradigm for global public health.
Public health decisions rely heavily on timely, granular data. For health conditions, such as cardiovascular disease or postpartum depression, that data shows us where to focus resources and support. For acute disease outbreaks, such as dengue or cholera, it can help inform urgent operational protocols and resource allocation. However, conventional epidemiological surveillance is often hindered by limitations in data: multi-year reporting lags, data siloed by rigid geopolitical boundaries, and data sparsity. Even without these limitations, traditional modeling approaches require extensive task-specific data collection and custom data engineering pipelines that are difficult to deploy during rapid outbreaks or in resource-constrained settings.
To address these systemic bottlenecks, we introduce a new paradigm in public health leveraging planetary geospatial foundation models. Using Google Earth AI’ s Population Dynamics Foundation Model (PDFM) as a proof-of-concept, we demonstrate how self-supervised, pre-trained representations of "place" can be integrated directly into existing health sciences and epidemiological workflows as plug-and-play inputs — enhancing the statistical and machine learning (ML) models epidemiologists already use, rather than building new pipelines from scratch. PDFM compresses privacy-preserving search trends, human mobility, built-environment density, and environmental determinants into location embeddings. Without requiring task-specific fine-tuning, these off-the-shelf location embeddings matched or improved on conventional inputs across a wide variety of disease domains, geographic settings, and epidemiological tasks.
Part of Google Earth AI — our suite of geospatial models connecting satellite imagery, weather, anonymous search trends, human mobility, and other population dynamics — PDFM uses self-supervised learning to synthesize the following diverse, privacy-preserving signals into compact, versatile embeddings that serve as “fingerprints” for locations refreshed at a monthly cadence:
Rather than requiring researchers to collect and process these raw data streams themselves, PDFM embeddings can be easily plugged into existing ML workflows to provide ready-to-use geospatial context.
Prior work showed that these embeddings are task-agnostic. Because these everyday signals capture the underlying social, behavioral, and environmental determinants of health, the same embeddings showed strong performance on filling gaps in a wide variety of CDC health metrics .
However, establishing a new paradigm for global health carries a higher burden of proof. To meet this standard, we set out to demonstrate the value of PDFM embeddings across a wider variety of health challenges, and in different environments across the globe.
Overview of Google Earth AI’s PDFM applied to a wide range of global health challenges.
To achieve this, our global health research partners facilitated independent evaluations across five distinct public health challenges — spanning diverse epidemiological tasks, resource settings, and disease types:
Mount Sinai Health System ; Boston Children’s Hospital
+36% relative gain in explained variance (0.159 0.216, statistically significant) by capturing cross-border mobility and information spillovers.
Cardiovascular disease (noncommunicable disease)
Department of Population Health, NYU Grossman School of Medicine
Contiguous United States (3,091 counties)
Comparable accuracy to census-based models for nowcasting (mean absolute error 18.7 vs 19.1 deaths per county; RMSE 46.00 vs 57.69; differences not statistically significant), making PDFM a timely stand-in when census data are outdated or unavailable.
University of Oxford and Tecnológico de Monterrey
Statistically significant 1-month forecast gain ( Δ Weighted Interval Score = -0.0051, lower is better) via TimesFM integration, concentrated in active transmission hotspots. Accuracy improved in up to 72% of active transmission municipalities.
Institute on Human Development and Disability, University of Washington
United States (CDC PRAMS) (332,970 respondents)
Transferable gain in risk prediction (AUC +0.0020 on a 0.62 baseline in seen states; +0.0038 in unseen states). Encoded area poverty (R² = 0.45). Recovers about 15% of the predictive signal of income and insurance records.
Cholera emergence ( water-borne disease )
Democratic Republic of the Congo (403 health zones, 89 weeks)
Statistically significant relative gains: +9.7% in Area Under the Precision-Recall Curve at 4 weeks; +18.1% Precision@5 (share of the model's five highest-risk zones each week that actually went on to have an outbreak) at 8 weeks, and +19.3% Precision@5 in endemic health zones.
Our evaluations show that while epidemiological models are constrained by sovereign borders, the outcomes they track are not. For example, in the 146 U.S. counties situated within 150 km of the Canadian border, domestic-only models often struggle to predict local vaccine uptake.
By supplementing U.S. county embeddings with Canadian Forward Sortation Area embeddings , researchers at the Mount Sinai Health System and Boston Children’s Hospital developed models that captured cross-border behavioral and mobility spillovers. item.page_text:
Analysis of more than three decades of satellite data suggests this year's very strong El Niño may have amplified Europe's hot, dry summer
The authors of a recent EUMETSAT case study say this year's extreme El Niño conditions may have partly amplified the hot, dry conditions seen across much of Europe in 2026.
“El Niño and its cold counterpart, La Niña, both influence winds and rainfall across the tropics in different ways, increasing the risk of drought in some regions and flooding in others,” said Rob Roebeling, Climate Product Expert at EUMETSAT, and an author of the case study. “They are opposite phases of the El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO), a natural cycle that is the biggest single source of year-to-year variation in the global climate. Effects in the tropics are well documented, although each event differs in strength and in the regions it affects. Their influence at higher latitudes, including Europe, is often less clear.”
Analysing data that include at least six El Niño and six La Niña events since 1991, the study found that El Niño summers tended to be warmer, sunnier and drier than normal across much of Europe, while La Niña summers tended to be cooler, cloudier and wetter. The difference in average conditions between El Niño and La Niña summers is too large to be explained by natural variation alone across a broad area of Europe. The authors report that heat and drought seen in Western and Central Europe in summer 2026 were broadly consistent with this pattern.
“This fits the idea that by altering large-scale patterns of rising and sinking air over the tropics, El Niño can trigger large scale meanders in jet streams that carry their influence on Europe, effects known as atmospheric teleconnections,” said Roebeling.
The Copernicus Climate Change Service (C3S) , implemented by the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) on behalf of the European Commission, reported that summer 2026 was Europe's third warmest on record and western Europe's warmest, 2.5°C above the 1991-2020 average, with a record 52% of the continent experiencing at least 'very strong' heat stress and near-record sea-surface temperatures observed across European seas.
El Niño effects come on top of the long-term warming from human-induced climate change, which the authors note remains the main driver of Europe's recent record-breaking summers, regardless of ENSO's phase – the continent's five warmest summers on record have all occurred since 2021.
“In El Niño events of the past 35 years, European winters were on average milder and wetter than normal, followed by warmer and cloudier springs. But other factors, such as blocking weather systems or unusually warm seas, can strengthen or reduce El Niño's influence, so how this winter and next year will turn out remains uncertain,” said Roebeling.
“The EUMETSAT case study draws on soil moisture and solar radiation climate normal and anomaly products from EUMETSAT’s Satellite Application Facilities. These recently introduced products adhere to World Meteorological Organization standards and reference periods and are available through EUMETSAT’s Climate Anomalies and Normals (CAN) service , alongside a range of other climate normal and anomaly products.”
The full case study is available on the EUMETSAT User Portal.
Investigating the impact of the El Niño Southern Oscillation on the European climate, using satellite data.
Introducing EUMETSAT’s new Climate Anomalies and Normals service.
New EUMETSAT service for tracking climate change is launched.

item.title: Mapped: The Most Walkable Cities in the U.S. & Canada
item.summary: San Francisco narrowly beats New York as the most walkable large city in the U.S. and Canada, while 90 of 130 cities remain car-dependent.
item.page_text:
Being able to walk to a grocery store, pharmacy, or café without getting in a car is an important consideration for many people choosing where to live.
But walkability depends on more than pedestrian-friendly streets. City boundaries also play a major role, helping explain why some smaller cities outperform much larger neighbors.
This map shows the 20 most walkable of the 130 U.S. and Canadian cities with at least 200,000 residents, using Walk Score’s 2021 city ranking, the latest it has published. Scores range from 0 to 100 and reflect proximity to everyday amenities, population density, and pedestrian-friendly infrastructure.
Even the highest-ranked cities fall short of Walk Score’s 90-point threshold for a “Walker’s Paradise,” where daily errands don’t require a car.
All eight Northeastern cities in the 130-city ranking score above 50, averaging 74.7, and six make the top 20: New York, Jersey City, Boston, Newark, Philadelphia, and Buffalo. The West has seven top-20 cities, five in California, but its 39 cities average only 48.7.
The table below ranks the 20 most walkable cities in the U.S. and Canada by Walk Score on a 0–100 scale:
City limits help explain some of the surprising results. Walk Score rates roughly every block in a city, weighted by where people live, so a city whose borders contain mostly its dense urban core can score higher than one that stretches into the suburbs.
That’s how Jersey City (86.6) ranks third, ahead of Boston (82.8). It covers just 15 square miles of land across the Hudson River from Manhattan, about one-twentieth the area of New York City (300 square miles), according to Census Bureau data .
Six other smaller cities in major metropolitan areas also make the top 20: Newark, Oakland, Long Beach, Arlington, Hialeah, and Santa Ana. Los Angeles shows the reverse pattern. Its 469 square miles include much of the San Fernando Valley, and it ranks 16th (68.6), behind neighboring Long Beach (73.3).
Vancouver ranks fifth (79.8). Across all 22 Canadian cities in the ranking, the average Walk Score is 47.6, nearly identical to the 47.8 average for the 108 U.S. cities.
Transit is where Canadian cities pull ahead. They average a Transit Score of 51.8, compared with 36.0 for U.S. cities, and 17 of the 22 score higher on transit than on walkability. Among the 101 U.S. cities with a Transit Score, only New York and Charlotte do.
The table below shows the Walk Score of all 130 cities, along with their Transit Score and Bike Score:
One notable omission from the top 20 is Toronto. Its Transit Score of 78.2 is second only to New York’s (88.6), yet its Walk Score of 61.0 ranks 28th, below Buffalo (66.6) and Pittsburgh (62.4).
City boundaries help explain the difference. Toronto’s current borders date to a 1998 merger that combined the old City of Toronto with five neighboring municipalities, including the postwar suburbs of North York, Scarborough, and Etobicoke. Its score now blends downtown’s dense streets with suburban neighborhoods laid out for driving, all served by the same subway and bus network.
The same split appears in the suburbs north of Toronto. Markham (34.5) and Vaughan (34.8) both rank among the 25 least walkable cities, yet Markham’s Transit Score of 49.3 is higher than that of all but 17 of the 101 U.S. cities.
Southern cities average a Walk Score of 41.0 and account for 13 of the 20 least walkable cities, including eight of the bottom 10.
Chesapeake, Virginia (21.3), Fayetteville, North Carolina (21.4), and Winston-Salem, North Carolina (22.5) rank last. They’re the only three cities scoring below 25, a range where almost all errands require a car.
Many of these cities have expansive boundaries. Chesapeake was created in 1963 when the small city of South Norfolk merged with what remained of Norfolk County, and it now covers 338 square miles of land. Jacksonville (25.6) and Nashville (28.8), also in the bottom 10, merged with their surrounding counties in 1968 and 1963, respectively.
North Carolina’s six cities in the ranking all fall in the bottom 14, from Raleigh (31.3) down to Fayetteville. From 1959 until 2011, state law let cities annex neighboring areas without the consent of landowners there. Charlotte (26.4) now covers 308 square miles of land, more than New York City (300).
Low walkability can have financial consequences for residents who depend on cars for everyday trips. Among households with auto loans, car ownership costs amount to 18.8% of median household income in Alabama and 17.8% in Florida, compared with 10.6% in Massachusetts, home to fourth-ranked Boston.
While these figures reflect statewide costs rather than individual cities, they highlight the broader financial importance of transportation options.
If you enjoyed today’s post, check out the global cities residents rate as most walkable on Voronoi.
